   "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document\n\nThis document covers «REGULATION (EU) 2023/1805 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 13 September 2023 on the use of renewable and low-carbon fuels in maritime transport, and amending Directive 2009/16/EC» It is an EU regulation and applies in the European Union; it was published on 22 September 2023 («22.9.2023 EN Official Journal of the European Union L 234/48»).\n\nStatements of what the text requires are marked *Legal Confirmation Required:* where the role of a freight forwarder or a charterer is not named in the text; the Commission guidance quoted in section 5 is cited as guidance, not as the Regulation. *Analytical inference:* the date of the next scheduled review is the Commission evaluation report set out in section 6.\n\n## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace\n\nThe Regulation caps the greenhouse gas intensity of the energy used on board large ships that call at EU ports. The effective date: «It shall apply from 1 January 2025, with the exception of Articles 8 and 9 which shall apply from 31 August 2024.»\n\n«This Regulation applies to all ships of above 5 000 gross tonnage that serve the purpose of transporting passengers or cargo for commercial purposes, regardless of their flag» It also reaches part of the extra-EU voyage: «one half of the energy used on voyages arriving at or departing from a port of call under the jurisdiction of a Member State, where the previous or the next port of call is under the jurisdiction of a third country»\n\nFor a freight forwarder that books ocean legs it matters on every Asia to Europe or transatlantic leg that touches an EU port, because the shipping line carries the compliance cost and recovers it through surcharges. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the Regulation names the shipping company, not the forwarder or the cargo owner, as the duty holder. Effect by cargo vertical (live events, artwork, luxury goods, film and television, automotive, humanitarian) requires carrier-specific data and is not stated by this source.\n\n## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action\n\nMONITORING: no action by a forwarder falls within 30 days of the document date. The annual compliance cycle runs on fixed days after each calendar year; the last step is that «By 30 June of the verification period, the verifier shall issue a FuelEU document of compliance for the ship concerned»\n\n*Operational implication:* an ocean procurement lead asks, in the next contract round, each shipping line on EU-touching lanes how it will recover FuelEU cost (a separate surcharge or inside the base rate) and whether the document of compliance for the previous year was issued; the decision that changes at each year end is whether a surcharge line is added to or removed from the quote.\n\n## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain\n\nThe duty holder is the company that operates the ship. «‘company’ means the shipowner or any other organisation or person such as the manager or the bareboat charterer, which has assumed the responsibility for the operation of the ship from the shipowner» «the company that has responsibility for the operation of the ship on 31 December of the reporting period shall be responsible for the compliance of the ship with the requirements set out in Articles 4 and 6 for the entire reporting period»\n\nA freight forwarder, an NVOCC and a cargo owner are not named. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a time charterer that is not the bareboat charterer carries any duty is not stated in these passages and should be confirmed with counsel; a forwarder that books slots sits downstream of the shipping line.\n\n## 5. Authoritative Guidance Document Analysis\n\nThe Commission published questions and answers on the Regulation. Two answers bear on how shipping lines can comply. «Energy efficiency technologies, alone, are not directly relevant for the reduction of the GHG intensity of the energy used onboard.» «Onboard Carbon Capture and Storage is not part of the technologies contributing to compliance under FuelEU Maritime Regulation.»\n\n*Industry interpretation:* guidance of this kind is the Commission's reading; it is cited as guidance and is not part of the legal text.\n\n## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events\n\nThree dated events can change the picture. «By 31 December 2027, and every five years thereafter at the latest, the Commission shall report to the European Parliament and the Council the results of an evaluation as regards the functioning of th»\n\nThe subtarget for renewable fuels of non-biological origin is conditional: «If the share of RFNBO referred to in paragraph 2 is less than 1 % for the reporting period 2031, a subtarget of 2 % shall apply for such fuels in the yearly energy used on board by a ship from 1 January 2034»\n\nExemptions for island and outermost region voyages end on a fixed date: «No such exemptions shall apply beyond 31 December 2029.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the evaluation at the end of 2027 is the date at which the 2030 step and the 2034 subtarget could be re-opened; the text does not say what the Commission will propose, and the subtarget depends on a 2031 market share that cannot be known now.\n\n## 8. Substantive Requirements\n\nThe substantive requirement is a falling cap on the GHG intensity of ship energy, plus shore power at berth.\n\n- Limit: «by reducing the reference value of 91,16 grams of CO 2 equivalent per MJ by the following percentage: — 2 % from 1 January 2025; — 6 % from 1 January 2030; — 14,5 % from 1 January 2035; — 31 % from 1 January 2040; — 62 % from 1 January 2045; — 80 % from 1 January 2050.»\n- Renewable fuel multiplier: «from 1 January 2025 to 31 December 2033 a multiplier of ‘2’ can be used to reward the ship for the use of RFNBO»\n- Shore power in covered ports: «From 1 January 2030, a ship moored at the quayside in a port of call which is covered by Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 and which is under the jurisdiction of a Member State shall connect to OPS and use it for all its electrical power demand at berth.»\n- Shore power elsewhere: «From 1 January 2035, a ship moored at the quayside in a port of call which is not covered by Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1804»\n- Penalty basis: «5. 41 000 6. Is 1 metric ton of VLSFO that is equivalent to 41 000 MJ 7. 2 400 8. Is the amount to be paid in EUR per equivalent metric ton of VLSFO»\n- Monitoring plan: «By 31 August 2024, companies shall submit to the verifiers a monitoring plan for each of their ships»\n- Condition on the renewable subtarget: «the subtarget provided for in paragraph 3 shall not apply»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the cap steps down by percentages from 2025 to 2050, so the cost of staying inside it rises with each step and the price of low-carbon fuels sets how much of that cost a shipping line passes on; the penalty is stated per equivalent metric ton of a reference fuel, and the text gives no per-container figure.\n\nNo phase-in is stated outside the dated percentages above. No exceptions are stated in Article 4. No scope limits are stated in Article 4 beyond the ships and voyages of Article 2.\n\nObligations surveyed: 9; workspace-adjacent: 6; extracted as FACT: 7.\n\n## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations\n\nThe reporting duties sit with the shipping company: «By 31 January of the verification period, companies shall provide to the verifier a ship-specific report (the ‘FuelEU report’)» «By 30 June of the verification period, ships calling at a port under the jurisdiction of a Member State»\n\n*Legal Confirmation Required:* the text sets no registration or reporting duty for a freight forwarder; the FuelEU database is used by companies, verifiers and competent authorities.\n\n## 11. Operational System Requirements\n\nMONITORING: the operational system requirement for a forwarder is a quote field and a contract question, not a system build.\n\n- An ocean pricing lead adds a FuelEU surcharge line to the quote template, with a note whether it is separate from the base rate, and records the shipping line that charges it.\n- A procurement lead asks each shipping line in the next contract round whether it will charge for shore power use at berth from 2030 and how the charge is set.\n\n*Operational implication:* these two steps use only the dates the text states and no cost figure.\n\n## 14. Confirmed Regulatory Timeline\n\n- 13 September 2023: the Regulation is adopted at Strasbourg\n- 22 September 2023: the Regulation is published in the Official Journal\n- 31 August 2024: monitoring plans are due, and Articles 8 and 9 begin to apply\n- 1 January 2025: the Regulation applies, with a 2 % reduction below the reference value\n- 31 December 2027: Commission evaluation report\n- 31 December 2029: island and outermost region exemptions end at the latest\n- 1 January 2030: 6 % reduction below the reference value, and shore power use in covered ports\n- 31 December 2033: the renewable fuel multiplier of 2 ends\n- 1 January 2034: conditional subtarget of 2 % for renewable fuels of non-biological origin\n- 1 January 2035: 14,5 % reduction, and shore power use in other ports with available shore power\n- 1 January 2040: 31 % reduction\n- 1 January 2045: 62 % reduction\n- 1 January 2050: 80 % reduction\n\n## 15. Sources\n\n- publications.europa.eu: https://publications.europa.eu/resource/celex/32023R1805\n- transport.ec.europa.eu: https://transport.ec.europa.eu/news-events/news/landmark-agreement-towards-achieving-net-zero-emissions-global-shipping-2050-2025-04-11_en\n- transport.ec.europa.eu: https://transport.ec.europa.eu/transport-modes/maritime/decarbonising-maritime-transport-fueleu-maritime/questions-and-answers-regulation-eu-20231805-use-renewable-and-low-carbon-fuels-maritime-transport_en\n- eur-lex.europa.eu: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/summary/renewable-and-low-carbon-fuels-in-maritime-transport.html",

   "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document\n\nThis document covers «DIRECTIVE 2003/87/EC OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 13 October 2003» the EU Emissions Trading System. It is an EU directive; it applies in the European Union through national law. «in order to promote reductions of greenhouse gas emissions in a cost-effective and economically efficient manner» The text read is «Consolidated TEXT: 32003L0087 — EN — 01.03.2024», a documentation tool.\n\nStatements of what the text requires are marked *Legal Confirmation Required:* where the role of a freight forwarder, an NVOCC or a charterer is not named in the text. *Analytical inference:* the date of the next scheduled review is the set of Commission reports in section 6, the earliest being a report on smaller ships due by 31 December 2026.\n\n## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace\n\nThe Directive makes ships, aircraft and installations hold and surrender emission allowances for their verified emissions. For ocean freight the scope is stated in Article 3ga: «shall apply in respect of fifty percent (50 %) of the emissions from ships performing voyages departing from a port of call under the jurisdiction of a Member State and arriving at a port of call outside the jurisdiction of a Member State» and «one hundred percent (100 %) of emissions from ships performing voyages departing from a port of call under the jurisdiction of a Member State and arriving at a port of call under the jurisdiction of a Member State, and one hundred percent (100 %) of emissions from ships within a port of call under the jurisdiction of a Member State»\n\nThe effective date for maritime transport is set by the phase-in schedule: «Shipping companies shall be liable to surrender allowances according to the following schedule»\n\nFor a freight forwarder it matters on every ocean leg that touches an EU port and on air legs within the EU, because the carrier recovers the allowance cost through surcharges. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the Directive names the shipping company, aircraft operator or installation operator as the duty holder; no duty on a forwarder is stated, but Article 3gc allows the shipping company to recover cost from another entity (section 4). Effect by cargo vertical (live events, artwork, luxury goods, film and television, automotive, humanitarian) requires carrier-specific data and is not stated by this source.\n\n## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action\n\nMONITORING: no action falls within 30 days of the document date. The nearest dated step that touches ocean freight is «No later than 31 December 2026, the Commission shall present a report to the European Parliament and to the Council in which it shall examine the feasibility and economic, environmental and social impacts of the inclusion in this Directive of emissions from ships, including offshore ships, below 5 000 gross tonnage but not below 400 gross tonnage»\n\n*Operational implication:* an ocean procurement lead lists, before the end of the year, the feeder and coastal services booked in the last year whose vessels are between the two size limits, because those services are the ones that would be brought into scope; the decision that changes on 31 December 2026 is whether smaller-vessel legs carry an allowance cost line in future quotes.\n\n## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain\n\nThe duty holder for ocean legs is the shipping company. «shipping company’ means the shipowner or any other organisation or person, such as the manager or the bareboat charterer» The Directive then allows the cost to move by contract: «when the ultimate responsibility for the purchase of the fuel, or the operation of the ship, or both, is assumed by an entity other than the shipping company pursuant to a contractual arrangement, the shipping company is entitled to reimbursement from that entity for the costs arising from the surrender of allowances» «The shipping company shall remain the entity responsible for surrendering allowances as required under Articles 3gb and 12 and for overall compliance with the provisions of national law transposing this Directive.»\n\nA freight forwarder, an NVOCC and a cargo owner are not named. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder that books space or charters a vessel is an entity that has assumed responsibility for the purchase of the fuel or the operation of the ship is a threshold question set out in section 7.\n\n## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events\n\nSeveral dated Commission steps can change the cost of an allowance-based surcharge. The size report is in section 3. «No later than 30 September 2028, the Commission shall assess the appropriateness of extending the application of Article 3ga(3), second subparagraph, beyond 31 December 2030» «By 1 January 2028, the Commission shall carry out an evaluation regarding the application of this paragraph and submit the results of that evaluation in a report»\n\nThe supply of allowances narrows on a fixed path, «The linear factor shall be 4,3 % from 2024 to 2027 and 4,4 % from 2028.» and the next published quantity is «By 30 June 2027, the Commission shall publish the Union-wide quantity of allowances for 2028 and, if required, the adjusted linear reduction factor.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a smaller yearly quantity of allowances, with the factor rising from 2028, points to upward pressure on the allowance price over time; the sources give no price forecast, and the decision that changes on 30 June 2027 is whether quotes that run into 2028 should carry an allowance price escalator.\n\n## 7. Threshold Questions\n\nOne threshold question decides whether a party other than the shipping company can be asked to pay: what counts as taking over the operation of the ship. The text defines it: «‘Operation of the ship’ for the purposes of this Article means determining the cargo carried or the route and the speed of the ship.»\n\n*Legal Confirmation Required:* a forwarder that books slots on a liner service does not determine the route or the speed of the ship, while a party that charters a whole vessel and decides cargo or route may; the text does not apply the definition to a forwarder, so the placement of a forwarder in either case is not decided here and should be confirmed with counsel before a contract clause is written.\n\n## 8. Substantive Requirements\n\nThe substantive requirement is to hold and surrender allowances for verified emissions, with a penalty if not.\n\n- Surrender: «(c) each shipping company surrenders a number of allowances that is equal to its total emissions during the preceding calendar year, as verified in accordance with Article 3ge.»\n- Maritime phase-in: «(a) 40 % of verified emissions reported for 2024 that would be subject to surrender requirements in accordance with Article 12; (b) 70 % of verified emissions reported for 2025 that would be subject to surrender requirements in accordance with Article 12; (c) 100 % of verified emissions reported for 2026 and each year thereafter»\n- Derogation: «By way of derogation from paragraph 3, first subparagraph, point (c), shipping companies may surrender 5 % fewer allowances than their verified emissions»\n- Penalty: «The excess emissions penalty shall be EUR 100 for each tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent emitted for which the operator or aircraft operator has not surrendered allowances.» «The penalties set out in paragraph 3 shall also apply in respect of shipping companies.»\n- Indexation: «The excess emissions penalty relating to allowances issued from 1 January 2013 onwards shall increase in accordance with the European index of consumer prices.»\n- Support for eligible aviation fuels: «(a) 70 % of the remaining price differential between the use of fossil kerosene and hydrogen from renewable energy sources, and advanced biofuels» «(b) 95 % of the remaining price differential between the use of fossil kerosene and renewable fuels of non-biological origin compliant with Article 25 of Directive (EU) 2018/2001, used in aviation»\n- Border adjustment: «From 2034, no CBAM factor shall apply.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the excess emissions penalty of EUR 100 per tonne is a ceiling reference on the cost of not surrendering, and it rises with consumer prices; the phase-in to 100 % for 2026 means the full allowance cost is carried on 2026 emissions and after, so ocean surcharges built on the partial years understate the later cost.\n\nNo phase-in is stated for aviation outside the dated steps above. No exceptions are stated in Article 16(3). No scope limits are stated in Article 16(3) beyond the operators, aircraft operators and shipping companies it names.\n\nObligations surveyed: 9; workspace-adjacent: 7; extracted as FACT: 9.\n\n## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations\n\nThe reporting duties sit with shipping companies and administering authorities: «the administering authority in respect of a shipping company shall ensure that a shipping company under its responsibility monitors and reports the relevant parameters during a reporting period»\n\n*Legal Confirmation Required:* the text sets no registration or reporting duty for a freight forwarder; whether a party that takes over operation under Article 3gc inherits any data duty is not stated.\n\n## 11. Operational System Requirements\n\nMONITORING: the operational system requirement for a forwarder is a quote field and a contract clause.\n\n- An ocean pricing lead adds an emissions allowance surcharge line to the quote template, with the allowance price and date used, and records the shipping line that charges it.\n- A contract lead asks counsel whether a vessel charter or slot agreement should say who bears the cost under Article 3gc, before the next charter or slot agreement is signed.\n\n*Operational implication:* both steps use only the provisions quoted and no allowance price.\n\n## 14. Confirmed Regulatory Timeline\n\n- 13 October 2003: the Directive is adopted\n- 1 January 2013: the penalty indexation begins for allowances issued from this date\n- 2024: maritime transport enters with 40 % of verified emissions\n- 2025: 70 % of verified emissions\n- 2026: 100 % of verified emissions\n- 31 December 2026: Commission report on smaller ships\n- 30 June 2027: Commission publishes the Union-wide quantity of allowances for 2028\n- 1 January 2028: Commission evaluation report\n- 2028: the linear factor rises to 4,4 %\n- 30 September 2028: Commission assesses extending Article 3ga(3)\n- 2034: no CBAM factor applies\n\n## 15.    "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document\n\nThis document covers «Directive (EU) 2023/959 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 May 2023 amending Directive 2003/87/EC establishing a system for greenhouse gas emission allowance trading within the Union and Decision (EU) 2015/1814» It is an EU directive; it applies in the European Union through national law, and it was adopted as stated: «Done at Strasbourg, 10 May 2023.»\n\nStatements of what the text requires are marked *Legal Confirmation Required:* where the role of a freight forwarder is not named in the text. *Analytical inference:* the date of the next scheduled review is the Commission report of 31 December 2026 set out in section 6.\n\n## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace\n\nThis Directive revises the EU Emissions Trading System: it adds maritime transport, tightens the cap and creates a second system for buildings and road transport fuels. The effective date: «The new rules entered into force on 5 June 2023.»\n\nIt is addressed to Member States, so it applies as national law once transposed: «Member States shall bring into force the laws, regulations and administrative provisions necessary to comply with Article 1 of this Directive by 31 December 2023. They shall apply those measures from 1 January 2024.» «However, Member States shall bring into force the laws, regulations and administrative provisions necessary to comply with the following articles by 30 June 2024»\n\nFor a freight forwarder it matters on ocean legs touching EU ports and, from the second system, on the price of road fuel that carriers buy. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the Directive is addressed to the Member States and names no duty on a forwarder. Effect by cargo vertical (live events, artwork, luxury goods, film and television, automotive, humanitarian) requires carrier-specific data and is not stated by this source.\n\n## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action\n\nMONITORING: no action falls within 30 days of the document date. The first maritime surrender date has passed: «Shipping companies must surrender (use) their first ETS allowances by 30 September 2025 for emissions reported in 2024.» Later surrender dates follow the same annual rule.\n\n*Operational implication:* an ocean pricing lead checks, before the next quote run, that the quote template shows the allowance surcharge as a separate line with the allowance price and date used; the decision that changes at each surrender date is whether the surcharge for the preceding year is trued up in the next contract round.\n\n## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain\n\nThe duty holders are Member States for transposition, shipping companies for ocean legs, and, in the new second system, regulated entities that release fuels for consumption, which include road transport fuel suppliers. «From 1 January 2028, Member States shall ensure that, by 31 May each year, the regulated entity surrenders an amount of allowances covered by this Chapter that is equal to the regulated entity’s total emissions, corresponding to the quantity of fuels released for consumption pursuant to Annex III, during the preceding calendar year»\n\nThe cost is expected to move down the chain: «From 1 January 2028, Member States shall ensure that, by 30 April each year until 2030, each regulated entity reports the average share of costs related to the surrender of allowances under this Chapter which it passed on to consumers for the preceding year.»\n\nA freight forwarder is not named. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder that buys fuel for its own trucks falls within the regulated entity concept is not stated in these passages and should be confirmed with counsel; a forwarder that buys road legs sees the cost through the carrier's fuel price.\n\n## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events\n\nDated steps still ahead: «No later than 31 December 2026, the Commission shall present a report to the European Parliament and to the Council in which it shall examine the feasibility and economic, environmental and social impacts of the inclusion in this Directive of emissions from ships, including offshore ships, below 5 000 gross tonnage but not below 400 gross tonnage» «By 31 July 2026, the Commission shall report to the European Parliament and to the Council on the following matters»\n\nThe scope widens on dated days: «From 1 January 2026 and 1 January 2027 respectively, the quantity of allowances shall be increased to take into account the coverage of greenhouse gas emissions other than CO 2 emissions from maritime transport activities and the coverage of emissions of offshore ships»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the report on smaller ships and the offshore step both extend the number of vessels that carry an allowance cost; the sources do not say what the Commission will propose, and the decision that changes on 31 December 2026 is whether smaller feeder and coastal legs get an allowance cost line in future quotes.\n\n## 8. Substantive Requirements\n\nThe new substantive requirements are a second allowance system for building and road transport fuels, a phase-in for ships, and a lower cap.\n\n- Second system monitoring and reporting: «Member States shall ensure that each regulated entity monitors for each calendar year from 2025 the emissions corresponding to the quan tities of fuels released for consumption pursuant to Annex III. They shall also ensure that each regulated entity reports those emissions to the competent authority in the following year, starting in 2026»\n- Second system surrender: see section 4, «From 1 January 2028, Member States shall ensure that, by 31 May each year, the regulated entity surrenders an amount of allowances covered by this Chapter that is equal to the regulated entity’s total emissions, corresponding to the quantity of fuels released for consumption pursuant to Annex III, during the preceding calendar year»\n- Price stability: «Where the average price of allowances referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article exceeds a price of EUR 45 for a period of two consecutive months, 20 million allowances covered by this Chapter shall be released from the market stability reserve»\n- National tax derogation: «Until 31 December 2030, by way of derogation from paragraphs 1 and 2 of this Article, where a regulated entity established in a given Member State is subject to a national carbon tax in force for the years 2027 to 2030»\n- Cap path: «The linear factor shall be 4,3 % from 2024 to 2027 and 4,4 % from 2028.»\n- Maritime phase-in: «(a) 40 % of verified emissions reported for 2024 that would be subject to surrender requirements in accordance with Article 12; (b) 70 % of verified emissions reported for 2025 that would be subject to surrender requirements in accordance with Article 12; (c) 100 % of verified emissions reported for 2026 and each year thereafter»\n- Border adjustment: «From 2034, no CBAM factor shall apply.»\n- Permit: «Member States shall ensure that, from 1 January 2025, no regulated entity carries out the activity referred to in Annex III unless that regulated entity holds a permit issued by a competent authority»\n- Scope of the second system: «the emissions corresponding to the quan tities of fuels released for consumption pursuant to Annex III»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the second system puts a carbon cost on road diesel from the surrender start, and the price-stability release at EUR 45 limits the first years' price; the text does not state a diesel price effect, so no pence-per-litre figure is given.\n\nNo phase-in is stated outside the dated steps above. No exceptions are stated in Article 5. No scope limits are stated in Article 5 beyond the entry into force.\n\nObligations surveyed: 7; workspace-adjacent: 5; extracted as FACT: 8.\n\n## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations\n\nThe reporting duties sit with regulated entities, shipping companies and Member States: «Member States shall ensure that each regulated entity monitors for each calendar year from 2025 the emissions corresponding to the quan tities of fuels released for consumption pursuant to Annex III. They shall also ensure that each regulated entity reports those emissions to the competent authority in the following year, starting in 2026» «From 1 January 2028, Member States shall ensure that, by 30 April each year until 2030, each regulated entity reports the average share of costs related to the surrender of allowances under this Chapter which it passed on to consumers for the preceding year.»\n\nThe penalty summary is a gap in this item: the captured text of the amending Directive states no penalty amount. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the text sets no registration or reporting duty for a freight forwarder.\n\n## 11. Operational System Requirements\n\nMONITORING: the operational system requirement for a forwarder is a quote field and a contract question.\n\n- A road pricing lead adds a fuel cost line to road quotes that can show a carbon cost component once a carrier passes it on, and records the carrier's stated basis.\n- An ocean procurement lead asks each shipping line in the next contract round how it recovers allowance cost and whether it will report the passed-on share, since regulated entities must report the average share passed on to consumers.\n\n*Operational implication:* both steps use only the provisions quoted and no allowance price.\n\n## 14. Confirmed Regulatory Timeline\n\n- 10 May 2023: the Directive is adopted at Strasbourg\n- 5 June 2023: the new rules enter into force\n- 31 December 2023: transposition deadline for Article 1\n- 1 January 2024: Member States apply the measures\n- 30 June 2024: transposition deadline for the buildings and road transport provisions\n- 30 September 2025: first maritime surrender date, for emissions reported in 2024\n- 1 January 2025: a permit is required for regulated entities in the second system\n- 2025: monitoring of fuel emissions begins in the second system\n- 1 January 2026: quantity of allowances increases for non-CO2 gases from ships\n- 31 July 2026: Commission reports\n- 31 December 2026: Commission report on smaller ships\n- 1 January 2027: quantity of allowances increases for offshore ships\n- 1 January 2028: second system surrender begins\n- 31 December 2030: national carbon tax derogation ends\n- 2034: no CBAM factor applies\n\n## 15.    "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document\n\nThis document covers «Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 September 2023 on the deployment of alternative fuels infrastructure, and repealing Directive 2014/94/EU» It is an EU regulation and applies in the European Union. It was published on 22 September 2023 («OJ L 234, 22.9.2023»). «The specific objectives of the Regulation are: to ensure minimum infrastructure to support the required uptake of alternative fuel vehicles across all transport modes and in all EU Member States to meet the EU’s climate objectives; to ensure full interoperability of the infrastructure; and to ensure comprehensive user information and adequate payment options at alternative fuels infrastructure.»\n\nStatements of what the text requires are marked *Legal Confirmation Required:* where a freight forwarder's role is not named in the text; statements that go beyond the text are marked as analysis. *Analytical inference:* the date of the next scheduled review is the Commission review of this Regulation set out in Article 24, described in section 6.\n\n## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace\n\nThe Regulation sets minimum recharging and refuelling infrastructure that each Member State has to deploy. The effective date is 13 April 2024: «The regulation is applicable since 13 April 2024.» «This Regulation shall be binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States.» «The regulation sets a number of mandatory national targets for the deployment of alternative fuels infrastructure in the EU, for road vehicles, vessels and stationary aircraft.»\n\nFor a freight forwarder it matters on three modes: heavy-duty road charging on the main EU road network, shore-side electricity for container ships in ports, and hydrogen refuelling. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the targets are addressed to Member States; no duty on a forwarder is stated, so the effect on a forwarder is through the carriers it uses and the infrastructure they can reach. Effect by cargo vertical (live events, artwork, luxury goods, film and television, automotive, humanitarian) requires carrier-specific data and is not stated by this source.\n\n## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action\n\nMONITORING: no action falls within 30 days of the document date. The nearest dated step is the Commission review, which falls on a date about two months away. «By 31 December 2026 and every five years thereafter, the Commission shall review this Regulation.»\n\n*Operational implication:* a regulatory lead who wants the forwarder's lane needs reflected in the review prepares a short position on the heavy-duty targets before the end of 2026; the decision that changes on that date is whether the heavy-duty charging targets are kept, raised or re-based.\n\n## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain\n\nThe duty holders in the text are Member States and the operators and owners of recharging and refuelling points. «Member States shall ensure a minimum coverage of publicly accessible recharging points dedicated to heavy-duty electric vehicles in their territory.» «By 14 April 2025, operators of publicly accessible recharging points and refuelling points for alternative fuels, or, in accordance with the arrangements between them, the owners of those points, shall ensure the availability of static data and dynamic data»\n\nA freight forwarder is not named. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder that owns or operates its own depot charging counts as an operator for the data duty is not stated and should be confirmed with counsel; a forwarder that buys road legs sits downstream of the carrier and the charging operator.\n\n## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events\n\nTwo Commission reports are set in Article 24. «By 31 December 2024, the Commission shall submit to the European Parliament and to the Council a technology and market-readiness report dedicated to heavy-duty vehicles.» The second is the review: «whether the traffic thresholds referred to in Article 3(6) and (7), in Article 4(4) and (5) and in Article 6(4) are still relevant»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the traffic thresholds decide where the Member State derogations on heavy-duty charging pools apply, so a change in them would change which road sections must have the full pool power; the captured text does not say what the Commission will propose.\n\n## 8. Substantive Requirements\n\nThe heavy-duty charging targets are set by Article 4(1) in dated steps. Member States have to ensure each of the following.\n\n- «(a) by 31 December 2025, along at least 15 % of the length of the TEN-T road network, publicly accessible recharging pools dedicated to heavy-duty electric vehicles are deployed in each direction of travel and that each recharging pool offers a power output of at least 1 400 kW and includes at least one recharging point with an individual power output of at least 350 kW;»\n- «(b) by 31 December 2027, along at least 50 % of the length of the TEN-T road network, publicly accessible recharging pools dedicated to heavy-duty electric vehicles are deployed in each direction of travel and that each recharging pool: (i) along the TEN-T core road network, offers a power output of at least 2 800 kW and includes at least two recharging points with an individual power output of at least 350 kW; (ii) along the TEN-T comprehensive road network, offers a power output of at least 1 400 kW and includes at least one recharging point with an individual power output of at least 350 kW;»\n- «(c) by 31 December 2030, along the TEN-T core road network, publicly accessible recharging pools dedicated to heavy-duty electric vehicles are deployed in each direction of travel with a maximum distance of 60 km between them and that each recharging pool offers a power output of at least 3 600 kW and includes at least two recharging points with an individual power output of at least 350 kW;»\n- «(d) by 31 December 2030, along the TEN-T comprehensive road network, publicly accessible recharging pools dedicated to heavy-duty electric vehicles are deployed in each direction of travel with a maximum distance of 100 km between them and each recharging pool offers a power output of at least 1 500 kW and includes at least one recharging point with an individual power output of at least 350 kW;»\n- «(e) by 31 December 2027, in each safe and secure parking area at least two publicly accessible recharging stations dedicated to heavy-duty electric vehicles with an individual power output of at least 100 kW are deployed;»\n- «(f) by 31 December 2030, in each safe and secure parking area at least four publicly accessible recharging stations dedicated to heavy-duty electric vehicles with an individual power output of at least 100 kW are deployed;»\n- «(g) by 31 December 2025, in each urban node publicly accessible recharging points dedicated to heavy-duty electric vehicles with an aggregated power output of at least 900 kW are deployed, provided by recharging stations with an individual power output of at least 150 kW;»\n- «(h) by 31 December 2030, in each urban node publicly accessible recharging points dedicated to heavy-duty electric vehicles with an aggregated power output of at least 1 800 kW are deployed, provided by recharging stations with an individual power output of at least 150 kW.»\n\nDerogations and method: «By way of derogation from paragraph 1 of this Article, along roads of the TEN-T network with a total annual average daily traffic of fewer than 2 000 heavy-duty vehicles and where the deployment of infrastructure cannot be justified in socio-economic cost-benefit terms» «The calculation of the percentage of the length of TEN-T road network referred to in paragraph 1, points (a) and (b), shall be based on the following elements»\n\nConditions and scope changes: «However, Member States should, subject to Union State aid rules, be able to support the deployment of the necessary publicly accessible recharging infrastructure» The review may also change scope: «a possible extension of the scope of this Regulation to other ship types following relevant adjustments in other relevant Union legal acts»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the steps run end 2025, end 2027 and end 2030 and rise in power and in network coverage, so heavy-duty charging capacity on the main corridors is set to grow in three dated steps; the text states no penalty for a Member State that misses a step.\n\nObligations surveyed: 10; workspace-adjacent: 8; extracted as FACT: 12.\n\n## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations\n\nThe reporting duties in the text sit with Member States and operators: «Member States shall review those cases every two years as part of the national progress reporting referred to in Article 15.» «By 14 April 2025, operators of publicly accessible recharging points and refuelling points for alternative fuels, or, in accordance with the arrangements between them, the owners of those points, shall ensure the availability of static data and dynamic data»\n\nThe penalty summary is a gap: the captured text states no penalty or sanction. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the national implementing rules and any enforcement route are outside the captured text.\n\n## 11. Operational System Requirements\n\nMONITORING: the operational system requirement for a forwarder is a lane-planning field, not a system change.\n\n- A procurement lead adds to the road carrier onboarding form a field for the heavy-duty charging the carrier relies on and the TEN-T section it runs, so that coverage steps in Article 4 can be matched to the lane.\n- A regulatory lead keeps a dated watch item for 31 December 2026, the review date set in Article 24.\n\n*Operational implication:* these two steps use only the dates the text states and no cost figure.\n\n## 14. Confirmed Regulatory Timeline\n\n- 22 September 2023: the Regulation is published in the Official Journal\n- 13 April 2024: the Regulation begins to apply\n- 2025: first heavy-duty charging step, with pools along part of the TEN-T road network\n- 2027: second heavy-duty charging step, with wider network coverage\n- 31 December 2026: Commission review of the Regulation\n- 2030: third heavy-duty charging step, with pool spacing and power at full level\n\n## 15. Sources\n\n- eur-lex.europa.eu: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1804/oj\n- eur-lex.europa.eu: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32023R1804\n- transport.ec.europa.eu: https://transport.ec.europa.eu/transport-themes/clean-transport/alternative-fuels-sustainable-mobility-europe/alternative-fuels-infrastructure_en\n- eur-lex.europa.eu: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401610",

   "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document\n\nThis document covers «COMMISSION DELEGATED REGULATION (EU) 2025/656 of 2 April 2025 amending Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards standards for wireless recharging, electric road system, vehicle-to-grid communication and hydrogen supply for road transport vehicles» It is an EU instrument and applies in the European Union. «Official Journal of the European Union EN L series 2025/656 18.6.2025»\n\nThe delegated act exists because «The Commission may amend Annex II on technical specifications of Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 to introduce new technical specifications or update references to the standards set out in that Annex to enable full technical interoperability of the recharging and refuelling infrastructure in terms of physical connections, communication exchanges and access for persons with reduced mobility.»\n\nStatements of what the text requires are marked *Legal Confirmation Required:* where the role of a freight forwarder is not named in the text; statements that go beyond the text are marked as analysis.\n\n## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace\n\nThe Regulation changes the technical standards that recharging points must meet under the EU charging regulation. «This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union . It shall apply from 8 January 2026.» «This Regulation shall be binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States.»\n\nIt matters to a freight forwarder that sells road legs because the connectors and communication standards decide whether a truck can use a given public charging point: «Direct current (DC) high-power recharging points for recharging infrastructure capable of supplying electricity to both light- and heavy-duty electric vehicles shall be equipped, for interoperability purposes, at least with vehicle connectors of the combined charging system “Combo 2” for Mode 4 recharging as described in standard EN IEC 62196-3:2022.»\n\n*Legal Confirmation Required:* the text sets standards for recharging points; it names no duty on a freight forwarder or a haulier, so any effect on a forwarder is through the road carriers it contracts and the charging they use. Effect by cargo vertical (live events, artwork, luxury goods, film and television, automotive, humanitarian) requires carrier-specific data and is not stated by this source.\n\n## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action\n\nMONITORING: no action falls within 30 days of the document date; the nearest dated change is a standard that applies to newly installed or renovated points from 1 January 2027. «Publicly accessible recharging points for alternating current (AC) and direct current (DC) for light- and heavy-duty electric vehicles installed or renovated from 1 January 2027 shall comply, for interoperability purposes, at least with standard EN ISO 15118-20:2022»\n\n*Operational implication:* a procurement lead who tenders road legs that rely on public heavy-duty charging asks, before the end of the year, whether the charging relied on was installed or renovated from 1 January 2027 and so must support the newer vehicle-to-grid standard; the decision that changes on 1 January 2027 is which charging counts as compliant for new points.\n\n## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain\n\nThe compliance chain in the text runs through the people who build and run recharging points. «Operators and manufacturers of both publicly accessible and private recharging points specifically for Mode 3 and 4 recharging for electric vehicles»\n\nA freight forwarder is not named in the text. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder that owns or operates its own depot charging is an operator in the sense of the text is not stated and should be confirmed with counsel; a forwarder that buys road legs sits downstream of the carrier and the carrier's charging provider.\n\n## 8. Substantive Requirements\n\nThe substantive requirements are technical standards set by date of installation or renovation.\n\n- Definitions: «“installed” means the initial placement of all relevant recharging point equipment, including hardware, software and associated electrical infrastructure, such as electricity supply connections, transformers, and other electrical systems, to enable the recharging of electric vehicles; (b) “renovated” means a major or complete replacement of relevant recharging point equipment.»\n- Buses and connectors from 8 January 2026: «alternating current (AC) normal-power recharging points and high-power recharging points for electric buses that are installed or renovated from 8 January 2026 shall be equipped, for interoperability purposes, at least with connectors of Type 2 for Mode 3 recharging as described in standard EN IEC 62196-2:2022;»\n- Vehicle-to-grid communication for public points from 8 January 2026: «The publicly accessible recharging points for alternating current (AC) and direct current (DC) for light- and heavy-duty electric vehicles installed or renovated from 8 January 2026 shall comply, for interoperability purposes, at least with the following standards»\n- Existing equipment: «direct current (DC) normal-power recharging points installed before that date shall continue to comply with standard EN IEC 62196-3:2014 until they are renovated»\n- Private points from 1 January 2027: «Private recharging points for alternating current (AC) and direct current (DC) electric light- and heavy-duty electric vehicles installed or renovated from 1 January 2027 shall comply, for interoperability purposes, at least with the following standards»\n- Scope extensions: «Technical specifications for electric road system (ERS) for dynamic ground-level power supply through conductive rails for light- and heavy-duty electric vehicles»\n\n*Analytical inference:* for a forwarder the practical content is a split in time: points installed or renovated from 8 January 2026 follow one standard set, points installed or renovated from 1 January 2027 a newer one, and older points stay on the earlier standard until renovated.\n\nNo phase-in is stated in Articles 1 and 2 beyond the dates above. No exceptions are stated in Articles 1 and 2. No scope limits are stated in Articles 1 and 2 other than the installed-or-renovated dates.\n\nObligations surveyed: 6; workspace-adjacent: 3; extracted as FACT: 6.\n\n## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations\n\nThe text sets no registration or reporting obligation for freight forwarders or hauliers. It states technical standards for recharging points and no filing, notification or reporting duty in Articles 1 and 2. The penalty summary is a gap: the captured text states no penalty or sanction. *Legal Confirmation Required:* reporting duties under the parent charging regulation are outside the captured text and are not covered here.\n\n## 11. Operational System Requirements\n\nMONITORING: the operational system requirement for a forwarder is a data field, not a system change.\n\n- A procurement lead adds a field to the road carrier onboarding form recording whether the carrier's public heavy-duty charging was installed or renovated from 1 January 2027, and which vehicle-to-grid standard it supports.\n- A tender owner adds the same question to any tender that names a charging-dependent lane.\n\n*Operational implication:* these two steps use only the dates the text states and no cost figure.\n\n## 14. Confirmed Regulatory Timeline\n\n- 2 April 2025: the Regulation is adopted (\"Done at Brussels, 2 April 2025\")\n- 18 June 2025: the Regulation is published in the Official Journal\n- 8 January 2026: the Regulation begins to apply, and points installed or renovated from this date follow the standards in Annex II as replaced\n- 1 January 2027: the newer vehicle-to-grid standard is the standard for points installed or renovated from this date\n\n## 15. Sources\n\n- eur-lex.europa.eu: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32025R0656",

   "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document\n\nThis document covers Regulation (EU) 2019/1242 on CO2 emission performance standards for new heavy-duty vehicles, as it stands after the 2024 amendment, and applies in the European Union. «this Regulation sets CO 2 emission performance requirements for new heavy-duty vehicles whereby the specific CO 2 emissions of the Union fleet of new heavy-duty vehicles shall be reduced compared to the reference CO 2 emissions as follows: (a) for the reporting periods of the year 2025 onwards by 15 %» The 2019 text appeared as «L_2019198EN.01020201.xml 25.7.2019» in the Official Journal on 25 July 2019, and the amending act was adopted as stated: «Done at Brussels, 14 May 2024.»\n\nStatements of what the text requires are marked *Legal Confirmation Required:* where a freight forwarder's role is not named in the text. *Analytical inference:* the date of the next scheduled review is the Commission review set out in section 6; the 2019 reduction figures above are the original text and are superseded by the 2024 amendment in section 8.\n\n## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace\n\nThe Regulation sets the fleet CO2 standard that truck manufacturers have to meet for new heavy-duty vehicles. «Article 2 Scope 1. This Regulation shall apply to new heavy-duty vehicles of categories N 2 and N 3 that meet the following characteristics» The effective date of the amended targets is stated in the amending act: «It shall apply from 1 July 2024.»\n\nFor a freight forwarder that buys road legs, it matters because new truck supply and prices follow these standards. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the standards are addressed to manufacturers; no duty on a freight forwarder is stated, so any effect on a forwarder is through the carriers it uses. Effect by cargo vertical (live events, artwork, luxury goods, film and television, automotive, humanitarian) requires carrier-specific data and is not stated by this source.\n\n## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action\n\nMONITORING: no action falls within 30 days of the document date. The nearest dated step that touches a forwarder is the fleet operator report in mid-2027. «By 30 June 2027, the Commission shall submit to the European Parliament and to the Council a report which contains an analysis of the potential need for and impact of initiatives to increase the share of zero-emission heavy-duty motor vehicles owned or leased by large fleet operators.»\n\n*Operational implication:* a regulatory lead for a forwarder that owns or leases heavy trucks prepares a short fleet profile in the coming quarter; the decision that changes on 30 June 2027 is whether measures aimed at large fleet operators carry a fleet-size test.\n\n## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain\n\nThe duty holders in the text are manufacturers, Member States and the Commission. «Starting from 1 July 2020, and in each subsequent reporting period, the Commission shall determine for each manufacturer the average specific CO 2 emissions in g/tkm for the preceding reporting period»\n\nA freight forwarder is not named. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder that buys heavy trucks for its own fleet takes any role under the Regulation is not stated; a forwarder that buys road legs sits downstream of the carrier, which buys the vehicles.\n\n## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events\n\nTwo dated reviews bear on heavy-duty road freight. The first is this Regulation's own review: «By 31 December 2027, the Commission shall review the effectiveness and impact of this Regulation, in particular as regards the objective of climate neutrality at the latest by 2050»\n\nThe second sits in the charging regulation that the 2024 amendment pairs with these targets: «By 31 December 2026, the Commission shall assess the national policy framework notified by Member States pursuant to Article 14(11)»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the review of the Regulation is the point at which the 2030, 2035 and 2040 steps could be re-opened, and the charging policy framework assessment of 31 December 2026 is the earlier date at which the infrastructure side is read; the texts say nothing on what either will conclude.\n\n## 8. Substantive Requirements\n\nThe substantive requirement is a manufacturer fleet standard, with a premium for missing it.\n\n- Baseline: «shall be reduced by the following percentages compared to the average CO 2 emissions of the reporting period of the year 2019»\n- «45 % for all vehicle sub-groups other than vocational vehicles for the reporting periods of the years 2030 to 2034;»\n- «65 % for all vehicle sub-groups for the reporting periods of the years 2035 to 2039;»\n- «90 % for all vehicle sub-groups for the reporting periods of the year 2040 onwards.»\n- Premium: «Where a manufacturer is found, pursuant to paragraph 2, to have excess CO 2 emissions in a given reporting period from 2025 onwards, the Commission shall impose an excess CO 2 emissions premium, calculated in accordance with the following formula: (a) from 2025 to 2029, (Excess CO 2 emissions premium) = (Excess CO 2 emissions × 4 250 EUR/gCO 2 /tkm)»\n- «(b) from 2030 onwards, (Excess CO 2 emissions premium) = (Excess CO 2 emissions × 6 800 EUR/gCO 2 /tkm)»\n- Scope: «Article 2 Scope 1. This Regulation shall apply to new heavy-duty vehicles of categories N 2 and N 3»\n- Exception: «approved heavy-duty vehicles falling under Article 2(3), first subparagraph, point (b), of Regulation (EU) 2018/858 shall not be subject to the CO 2 emissions reduction targets»\n- Conditions on delegated powers: «The power to adopt delegated acts is conferred on the Commission subject to the conditions laid down in this Article»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the premium per gram of CO2 per tonne-kilometre rises between 2025 and 2030, so a manufacturer that misses the 2030 step pays a higher rate than a manufacturer that misses the 2025 step by the same amount; the text gives no per-vehicle price effect, so the effect on a truck price is not stated.\n\nNo phase-in is stated beyond the reporting-period steps above. \n\nObligations surveyed: 6; workspace-adjacent: 4; extracted as FACT: 9.\n\n## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations\n\nThe reporting duties in the text sit with manufacturers, Member States and the Commission, not with forwarders: «By 30 April each year, the Commission shall»\n\n*Legal Confirmation Required:* the detail of Member State reporting on registered vehicles is outside the passages quoted here.\n\n## 11. Operational System Requirements\n\nMONITORING: the operational system requirement for a forwarder is a procurement field, not a system change.\n\n- A procurement lead adds to the road carrier onboarding form a field for the share of zero-emission vehicles in the carrier's heavy-duty fleet and the year its fleet plan assumes, so that the 2030, 2035 and 2040 steps can be read against it.\n- A tender owner keeps dated watch items for 31 December 2026 and 30 June 2027 and 31 December 2027, the three dates in sections 3 and 6.\n\n*Operational implication:* these steps use only the dates the text states and no cost figure.\n\n## 14. Confirmed Regulatory Timeline\n\n- 25 July 2019: Regulation (EU) 2019/1242 is published in the Official Journal\n- 14 May 2024: Regulation (EU) 2024/1610 amends it, adopted at Brussels\n- 1 July 2024: the amending Regulation begins to apply\n- 2025: first reporting-period step, with a 15 % reduction for listed sub-groups and the first excess emissions premium rate\n- 31 December 2026: Commission assessment of national policy frameworks under the charging regulation\n- 30 June 2027: Commission report on large fleet operators\n- 31 December 2027: Commission review of the Regulation\n- 2030: 45 % reduction step and the higher premium rate\n- 2035: 65 % reduction step\n- 2040: 90 % reduction step\n- 2050: climate neutrality objective at the latest\n\n## 15. Sources\n\n- eur-lex.europa.eu: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32019R1242\n- eur-lex.europa.eu: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202401610\n- climate.ec.europa.eu: https://climate.ec.europa.eu/eu-action/transport-decarbonisation/road-transport/lorries-buses-and-coaches_en",

   "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document\n\nThis document covers an EU regulation that amends the CO2 standards for new heavy-duty vehicles and applies in the European Union. «Article 1\n\nAmendments to Regulation (EU) 2019/1242\n\nRegulation (EU) 2019/1242 is amended as follows» «This Regulation sets CO 2 emissions performance standards for new heavy-duty vehicles. Those standards contribute to achieving the Union’s climate-neutrality objective and the intermediate Union climate targets»\n\nIt was adopted at «Done at Brussels, 14 May 2024.» *Analytical inference:* the date of the next scheduled review is the Commission review of the amended Regulation set out in section 6. Statements of what the text requires are marked *Legal Confirmation Required:* where the role of a freight forwarder is not named in the text.\n\n## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace\n\nThe Regulation tightens the CO2 targets that truck and bus manufacturers have to meet for new vehicles. The effective date is stated in Article 5: «This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union .\nIt shall apply from 1 July 2024.» «This Regulation shall be binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States.»\n\nIt matters to a freight forwarder that buys road legs because the supply and price of new trucks follow these targets, and because the targets depend on charging: «The Union fleet-wide CO 2 emissions reduction targets laid down in this Regulation are complemented by the recharging and refuelling infrastructure requirements set out in Regulation (EU) 2023/1804»\n\n*Legal Confirmation Required:* the targets are addressed to manufacturers; no duty on a freight forwarder or a haulier is stated, so any effect on a forwarder is through the carriers it uses. Effect by cargo vertical (live events, artwork, luxury goods, film and television, automotive, humanitarian) requires carrier-specific data and is not stated by this source.\n\n## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action\n\nMONITORING: no action falls within 30 days of the document date. The nearest dated step that touches a forwarder is a Commission report on fleet operators in mid-2027. «By 30 June 2027, the Commission shall submit to the European Parliament and to the Council a report which contains an analysis of the potential need for and impact of initiatives to increase the share of zero-emission heavy-duty motor vehicles owned or leased by large fleet operators.»\n\n*Operational implication:* a regulatory lead for a forwarder that owns or leases heavy trucks prepares a short fleet profile (number of heavy-duty vehicles, share electric) in the coming quarter, so that the forwarder can respond to the report; the decision that changes on 30 June 2027 is whether initiatives aimed at large fleet operators come with a fleet-size test.\n\n## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain\n\nThe duty holders are manufacturers of new heavy-duty vehicles, measured as a Union fleet average. «The average CO 2 emissions of the Union fleet of new heavy-duty motor vehicles, other than special purpose vehicles, off-road vehicles and off-road special purpose vehicles shall be reduced by the following percentages compared to the average CO 2 emissions of the reporting period of the year 2019»\n\nA freight forwarder is not named. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder that buys heavy trucks for its own fleet takes any role under the Regulation is not stated; a forwarder that buys road legs sits downstream of the carrier, which buys the vehicles.\n\n## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events\n\nThe Regulation sets several Commission reports. Two have passed their dates, the report due on 30 June 2025 and the report due on 31 December 2025: «By 30 June 2025, the Commission shall submit to the European Parliament and to the Council a report which considers the need to facilitate the uptake on the Union market of heavy-duty vehicles which are retrofitted to become zero-emission heavy-duty vehicles, including by way of harmonised rules.» «the Commission shall by 31 December 2025 present a report to the European Parliament and to the Council with a comprehensive analysis of the need to further incentivise the uptake of advanced biofuels and biogas and renewable fuels of non-biological origin» The review that remains ahead is: «By 31 December 2027, the Commission shall review the effectiveness and impact of this Regulation, in particular as regards the objective of climate neutrality at the latest by 2050»\n\nThe 30 June 2027 report on large fleet operators is set out in section 3. *Analytical inference:* the review is the point at which the 2030, 2035 and 2040 steps could be re-opened, so it is the date that changes how far ahead a forwarder can plan truck availability; the text does not say what the review will propose. The captured pages do not say whether the 2025 reports were published.\n\n## 8. Substantive Requirements\n\nThe substantive requirement is a stepped reduction of manufacturer fleet CO2 against the 2019 reporting period.\n\n- «15 % for vehicle sub-groups 4-UD, 4-RD, 4-LH, 5-RD, 5-LH, 9-RD, 9-LH, 10-RD and 10-LH for the reporting periods of the years 2025 to 2029;»\n- «45 % for all vehicle sub-groups other than vocational vehicles for the reporting periods of the years 2030 to 2034;»\n- «65 % for all vehicle sub-groups for the reporting periods of the years 2035 to 2039;»\n- «90 % for all vehicle sub-groups for the reporting periods of the year 2040 onwards.»\n- Urban buses: «manufacturers shall comply with the 90 % and 100 % minimum shares of zero-emission heavy-duty vehicles in their fleet of new heavy-duty vehicles»\n- Data penalty: «The administrative fines shall be effective, proportionate and dissuasive and shall not exceed EUR 30 000 for each heavy-duty vehicle concerned by deviating or delayed data»\n- Exception for some approved vehicles: «approved heavy-duty vehicles falling under Article 2(3), first subparagraph, point (b), of Regulation (EU) 2018/858 shall not be subject to the CO 2 emissions reduction targets»\n- Conditions on delegated powers: «The power to adopt delegated acts is conferred on the Commission subject to the conditions laid down in this Article»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the percentages step up at 2030, 2035 and 2040, so the share of new trucks that must be zero or low emission rises in three steps; the captured text states the percentages and not the vehicle mix that meets them.\n\nNo phase-in is stated in Articles 1 and 5 beyond the dates above. No scope limits are stated in Article 5 other than the entry into force.\n\nObligations surveyed: 6; workspace-adjacent: 4; extracted as FACT: 8.\n\n## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations\n\nThe reporting duties in the text sit with manufacturers and Member States, not with forwarders. «The Commission may impose an administrative fine in each of the following cases»\n\nThe penalty summary is therefore limited: the fine cap in section 8 is the only amount stated, and the premium on excess CO2 emissions is a gap in the captured text. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the rules on the excess emissions premium are outside the captured text.\n\n## 11. Operational System Requirements\n\nMONITORING: the operational system requirement for a forwarder is a procurement field, not a system change.\n\n- A procurement lead adds to the road carrier onboarding form a field for the share of zero-emission vehicles in the carrier's heavy-duty fleet and the year its fleet plan assumes, so that the 2030, 2035 and 2040 steps can be read against it.\n- A tender owner keeps a dated watch item for 30 June 2027 and 31 December 2027, the report and review dates in the text.\n\n*Operational implication:* these steps use only the dates the text states and no cost figure.\n\n## 14. Confirmed Regulatory Timeline\n\n- 14 May 2024: the Regulation is adopted at Brussels\n- 1 July 2024: the Regulation begins to apply\n- 2025: first reporting-period step, with a 15 % reduction for listed sub-groups\n- 31 December 2025: Commission report on renewable fuels in heavy-duty vehicles\n- 30 June 2027: Commission report on large fleet operators\n- 31 December 2027: Commission review of the Regulation\n- 2030: 45 % reduction step\n- 2035: 65 % reduction step\n- 2040: 90 % reduction step\n- 2050: climate neutrality objective at the latest\n\n## 15.    "body": "## 1. What's Moving and What Triggered It\n\nThe signal event is a price and volume reading for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), taken from two sources. On volume: «Approximately 2.4 billion litres (1.92 million tonnes) of SAF was produced in 2025 . This is almost double the 1.25 million litres (1 million tonnes) that was produced in 2024.» «SAF usage in 2025 represented 0.6% of the total fuel consumption by airlines, compared to 0.3% in 2024.»\n\nOn price: «Today, sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) generally costs between 2 and 5 times more than fossil jet fuel.» «The European Union Aviation Safety Agency estimated that the average production cost of SAF in 2024 ranged from €1,461 per tonne (for biofuels) to €7,695 per tonne (for e-fuels).» «We calculate that this is a cost premium of 2.1–10.6x compared with fossil jet fuel by converting fossil jet production costs from the International Energy Agency, reported in U.S. dollars per liter, into equivalent units.» «The cost of SAF is primarily driven by the cost of its feedstock.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the two readings together say that SAF volume is growing quickly from a very small base while its unit cost stays a multiple of fossil jet fuel. The sources do not give a dated price series, so no trend in the premium can be read from them.\n\n## 2. Who's Driving It and What They Want\n\nThe driving parties named in the sources are governments, airlines and two bodies that publish the numbers. «One of the most exciting areas in the field of aviation environmental action and a cornerstone of the commitment to zero carbon emissions is the increasing use of sustainable aviation fuel, commonly known as SAF.» «As of now, regions such as the United Kingdom and European Union have put SAF mandates in place with penalties for non-compliance; these are examples of a market pull.    "body": "## 1. What's Moving and What Triggered It\n\nThe signal event is the price of an EU emission allowance, which sets the carbon cost carried by ships and aircraft covered by the EU Emissions Trading System. «European Union €78.23 +1.93% -15.35%» The ICAP page reports the annual averages: «Average auction price (2025) EUR 73.43 (USD 82.97) Average secondary market price (2025) EUR 74.35 (USD 84.01)»\n\nThe system now reaches ocean freight: «In January 2024, it was extended to cover emissions from maritime transport»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the live price sits above both 2025 averages, while the year-to-date change is negative; the sources give no date for the live reading beyond the page capture, so the comparison is between a point reading and annual averages, not between two prices on the same basis.\n\n## 2. Who's Driving It and What They Want\n\nThe driving parties are the EU legislators who set the cap and the shipping and aviation operators who must hold allowances; the sources name no trading counterparties. «Cap or total emissions limit 1,185.4 MtCO2e (2026, electricity and heat generation, industrial manufacturing and maritime transport), 26.2 MtCO2e (2026, aviation)»\n\n«companies must surrender allowances equal to 40% of their verified 2024 CO 2 emissions and 70% for 2025.» «In aviation, free emission allowances for operators were down to 50% in 2025 and are fully phased out as of 2026.  In parallel, a per-tonne financial support for  sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) was introduced to  incentivise uptake while free allocations are phased out.»\n\n*Industry interpretation:* ICAP is a network of governments and public authorities that publishes system factsheets; its summary is cited as a secondary reading of the legislation.\n\n## 3. Expected Trajectory and Conversion Triggers\n\nThe conversion trigger the source names is the end of the stop-the-clock limit on aviation scope, which the page gives as the end of 2026. «This ‘stop-the-clock’ limited scope of the EU ETS for aviation was extended until the end of 2026.» The cap then tightens on a fixed path: «4.3% for 2024 to 2027 and 4.4% from 2028.»\n\n- 2026: the stop-the-clock limit on aviation scope runs until the end of 2026\n- 2028: the linear reduction factor rises to 4.4%\n\n*Analytical inference:* a tighter cap with a declining supply of free allowances points to a higher carbon cost per tonne for covered voyages and flights over time, but the sources give no price forecast, so the size of any move is not stated.\n\n## 4. Operational and Cost Implications If It Materializes\n\nFor a forwarder the allowance cost reaches the invoice through carrier surcharges on ocean and air legs that touch the EU. «Total revenue (2025) EUR 43.2 billion»\n\n*Operational implication:* where an ocean carrier or an airline prices an ETS surcharge from the allowance price, the live reading above and the 2025 averages bound the per-tonne cost; the sources do not state any carrier surcharge or how much of a voyage is covered, so the cost per container or per kilogram is not given here. The effect by cargo vertical (live events, artwork, luxury goods, film and television, automotive, humanitarian) requires carrier-specific data and is not stated by these sources.\n\n## 7. What the Workspace Should Do Now\n\nCOST ALERT: the action now is to fix the allowance price and date used in every quote that carries an ETS cost line.\n\n- A pricing lead in the ocean desk sets the ETS line of the next ocean quote run to a stated allowance price and date, and records the price used so a later quote can be compared.\n- A pricing lead in the air desk does the same for the air quote run and records which flights the carrier treats as covered.\n- A procurement lead asks each carrier in the next contract round how its ETS surcharge is indexed to the allowance price.\n\n*Operational implication:* these steps put the live reading against the 2025 averages in front of the person who sets the quote; the sources hold no surcharge schedule.\n\n## 8. What the Research Found\n\nThe finding is that the International Maritime Organization has no adopted global fuel standard or carbon price for shipping as of the assessment update of «26 Mar 2026». «The IMO failed to adopt the Net Zero Framework (NZF), a global fuel standard and carbon pricing mechanism, at the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s (MEPC) extraordinary session in October 2025.» «International shipping accounts for about 2.3% of global CO 2 emissions in 2023 (ICCT, 2025).» «With the current level of policy action, CO 2 emissions are projected to be between 729-768 MtCO 2 in 2030 (based on a voyage-based approach), only representing a 1-6% decrease below the reference emissions level in 2008.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the assessment is a rating of policy ambition by a tracker, not a regulatory text, and its numbers are projections; they say where emissions go against the 2008 reference level if no new measure is adopted, not what any rule requires.\n\n## 2. Why This Finding Matters Operationally and Commercially\n\nThe finding matters operationally because the global measure that would have set one rule for all ocean carriers was not adopted, so carriers stay under regional rules and their own fuel choices. «Instead of abandoning the NZF, governments decided to postpone the vote to October 2026.» «the measures promote a switch to LNG-powered ships, resulting in greater GHG emissions»\n\n*Operational implication:* an ocean forwarder cannot assume a single global carbon cost on bunker fuel from the IMO in the near term; the regional systems cited in other items remain the live pricing basis. Effect by cargo vertical (live events, artwork, luxury goods, film and television, automotive, humanitarian) requires carrier-specific data and is not stated by this source.\n\n## 3. What the Finding Changes for Strategy, Claims, or Decisions\n\nThe finding changes the planning assumption for ocean carbon cost: a global economic instrument expected from 2027 is not in force and its adoption is open. «Current policies put the shipping sector far off track from achieving the IMO’s target of reducing emissions by 20% and striving for 30% by 2030, with an implementation gap of 109–186 MtCO 2 .» «Agreed to a fuel-based target of at least 5%, striving for 10%, of the energy used in international shipping to come from zero and “near zero” emission fuels and technologies by 2030.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a freight forwarder that told clients to expect one global measure should state instead that the regional systems set the cost, and that the global measure depends on a vote the source places in October 2026.\n\n## 5. What the Research Found\n\nThe finding is an analysis of what the International Maritime Organization revised strategy implies for a ship's fuel choice. «A key milestone was reached in July 2023, when Member States of the International Maritime Organization (IMO), during its 80 th Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC80) meeting, agreed on a revised greenhouse gas (GHG) strategy.» «The strategy’s target of 70% (striving for 80%) reduction in absolute emissions would likely require the average ship to reduce its greenhouse gas (GHG) intensity by ~90% by 2040, when increased trade volumes are accounted for.» «More immediately, the strategy aims for 5-10% of the energy used in shipping in 2030 to have zero or near-zero GHG emissions.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the analysis turns percentage targets on absolute emissions into a per-ship intensity requirement; it is a reading by a maritime industry forum of the strategy text, not part of the strategy.\n\n## 2. Why This Finding Matters Operationally and Commercially\n\nThis matters operationally because fuel choice on ocean legs drives the surcharges and the carbon cost that reach a forwarder's invoice over the next decade. «Transition solutions now have a short window for commercial viability. The focus needs to be on scalable zero-emission fuels like e-ammonia, e-methanol, 1 and green hydrogen, as these will need to make up the majority of the sector’s fuel use by the late 2030’s.»\n\n*Operational implication:* an ocean forwarder asking carriers about their fuel plans should expect answers framed around e-ammonia, e-methanol and green hydrogen for new capacity; the analysis gives no price for any of them, so no cost is stated. Effect by cargo vertical (live events, artwork, luxury goods, film and television, automotive, humanitarian) requires carrier-specific data and is not stated by this source.\n\n## 3. What the Finding Changes for Strategy, Claims, or Decisions\n\nWhat the finding changes for decisions is the timing of the fuel and pricing measures that clients may ask about. The analysis treats 2025 as the year the measures were to be adopted. «The adoption of mid-term measures in 2025, including a fuel standard and a GHG pricing mechanism, will be crucial.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a statement made in 2023 about 2025 cannot be read as the position today; the other IMO item in this set records that the vote slipped, so this analysis is used only for the intensity arithmetic, not for the adoption date.\n\n## 5. What the Finding Does Not Resolve\n\nWhat the finding does not resolve: «The adoption of mid-term measures in 2025, including a fuel standard and a GHG pricing mechanism, will be crucial.» is a condition the analysis states and does not settle, and the analysis does not say whether the pricing mechanism would be a levy or a market measure. The methodology limits are scope limits: «The current targets are benched against 2008 levels. Yet trade volumes have increased significantly since then» The evidence agreement signal and the source authority signal are not stated in the captured text.\n\n- 2018: the IMO initial strategy set the industry on a path to decarbonise\n- 2023: revised strategy agreed in July\n- 2025: mid-term measures to be adopted, per the analysis\n- 2030: indicative checkpoint year and the 5-10% zero-emission energy aim\n- 2040: indicative checkpoint year, with a 70% (striving for 80%) absolute emissions reduction\n\n## 6.
